{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Erythema toxicum neonatorum", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Transient neonatal pustular melanosis", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Neonatal acne", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Candida albicans cutaneous infection", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome", "confidence": 0.45}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.523, "reasoning": "In a newborn with onset of generalized rash within the first few days of life, benign self-limited conditions dominate the differential. Erythema toxicum neonatorum is the most common neonatal rash (present in ~40–70% of term infants), typically appearing on day 1–2 as erythematous macules/papules with central pustules, and carries high diagnostic confidence. Transient neonatal pustular melanosis is also common, especially in darker-skinned infants, presenting at birth or within 24 hours with sterile pustules that rupture to leave hyperpigmented macules; its early presentation aligns well. Neonatal acne (due to maternal androgen stimulation) usually appears after day 2–3 but can manifest earlier and is often facial-predominant though occasionally generalized. Cutaneous Candida is plausible—especially with risk factors like vaginal delivery, antibiotics, or prolonged membrane rupture—but typically shows satellite pustules and favors intertriginous areas; generalized involvement is less typical without immunocompromise, lowering confidence. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is rare in neonates (who are relatively protected by maternal antibodies), usually presents after day 3–5, and features widespread erythema, tenderness, and Nikolsky sign—not classic for a 1-day-old with isolated rash; thus it is included but assigned low confidence due to low pretest probability and potential severity if missed."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Erythema toxicum neonatorum", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Transient neonatal pustular melanosis", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Neonatal acne", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Miliaria rubra", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (early localized form)", "confidence": 0.42}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.523, "reasoning": "Erythema toxicum neonatorum is the most common benign neonatal rash, typically presenting on day 1–2 of life with erythematous macules/papules and central pustules, sparing palms/soles—highly consistent with this case (confidence 0.92). Transient neonatal pustular melanosis also presents in the first days with sterile pustules that rupture to leave hyperpigmented macules, often sparing palms/soles, and is more common in darker-skinned infants (0.85). Neonatal acne (papulopustular eruption due to maternal androgen stimulation) usually appears after day 2–3 but can begin on day 1; lesions are folliculocentric and non-inflammatory or mildly inflammatory, without systemic signs (0.78). Miliaria rubra (prickly heat) may occur in warm/humid environments or with overheating, presenting as small erythematous papules/pustules, but less commonly generalized and typically spares palms/soles—plausible but less characteristic (0.65). Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is unlikely given absence of Nikolsky sign, systemic toxicity, or mucosal involvement, and palm/sole sparing argues against classic SSSS (which often involves periorificial and flexural areas early, but palmar/planter involvement is typical in later stages); isolated early presentation is rare and would raise concern for sepsis—thus low confidence (0.42). Other entities like congenital syphilis, HSV, or candidiasis were deprioritized due to lack of vesicles, bullae, mucosal lesions, or risk factors, and because palms/soles are spared (syphilis and HSV often involve them)."}
